title: Against the Pinterest Classroom
author: Daniel Buck
summary: Daniel Buck, a research fellow at AEI and former English teacher and assistant principal, argues that heavily decorated 'Pinterest classrooms' are a symptom of a deeper pedagogical mistake: prioritizing engagement and aesthetics over learning conditions. Drawing on research showing that highly decorated walls increase student distraction and reduce learning gains, and that row-based seating doubles on-task behavior compared to group tables, Buck makes the case that classroom design is a small but real lever in academic achievement. The deeper critique is not about aesthetics but about the question teachers ask: 'How can I engage my students today?' instead of 'What are they going to learn?' The same impulse that fills classrooms with confetti shows up in lessons that prioritize glitter and razzmatazz over close reading, note-taking, and writing. Buck invokes Mike Schmoker's argument that simple, routine academic activities done well are more effective than elaborate activities, and argues for an orderly, purposeful classroom aesthetic—framed art, anchor charts, showcased student work—that signals to students that learning is a serious endeavor.
points: Research shows children are more distracted, more off-task, and show smaller learning gains in highly decorated classrooms than when decorations are removed—and the effect holds in real classrooms, not just laboratory conditions.
Studies of seating arrangements find that shifting from group tables to rows doubles on-task behavior, reduces disruption, and yields the greatest benefits for disruptive students.

The over-decorated classroom is a symptom of the engagement-first mindset: teachers asking 'How can I engage my students today?' instead of 'What are they going to learn, and how can I best facilitate that?'

Buck invokes cognitive load theory: visual noise in a classroom is analogous to trying to read in a chaotic airport—the excess stimuli compete with the content of instruction for limited working memory.

The practical standard is Schmoker's: versatile, routine academic activities—close reading, note-taking, discussion, writing—done well are more effective than elaborate, elaborately decorated ones; the classroom aesthetic should signal that learning is serious work.
quotes: We've all visited those classrooms. They look like 30-gallon bags full of confetti, crepe paper, and Elmer's glue exploded in the center. The bulletin boards are a mess of student work and neon posters, arts and crafts projects dangle from the ceiling, and groups of desks are buried in tassels and decorations.
children were more distracted, off task, and demonstrated smaller learning gains when "walls were highly decorated than when the decorations were removed.
students display higher levels of appropriate behaviour during individual tasks when they are seated in rows, with disruptive students benefiting the most.

The final end of any classroom is academic instruction and learning. Thus, all decisions must be made to that end. Materials need to be easily accessible. Teachers must be able to move about freely without obstruction. And student attention should be directed towards the front where instruction occurs—not to their friends or a collage of posters and crepe paper.

Underneath the pull toward an over-decorated classroom is a prioritizing of engagement, activity, or even fun, not learning. This same tendency then manifests in classroom activities that prioritize glitter, glue, and razzmatazz over academic work.

Lessons need not be particularly elaborate or complex. Teachers can build them around versatile (but underappreciated) routine academic activities such as close reading, note-taking, discussions, and writing prompts about content.... Done right, these activities never become dull.

I don't expect replacing a "Dream Big, Be Kind, You Matter" pastel post with a framed portrait of Lincoln will cause fourth grade reading score on NAEP suddenly to rise. But it will signal to students that in this particular classroom, at least, the work of learning history, science, literature, and the arts is treated as a serious endeavor.
